Beth-shean
beth-SHEE-an
proper noun
From the Hebrew beth she’an, “house of quiet” or “house of rest,” a city guarding the Jordan valley.

Biblical Definition

Beth-shean, also called Beth-shan, was a strong Canaanite city commanding the eastern end of the valley of Jezreel where it descends toward the Jordan. Though it lay within the allotment of Manasseh, the children of Manasseh could not at the first drive out its inhabitants, for the Canaanites would dwell in that land; and when Israel was strong, they put them to tribute but did not utterly expel them. So Beth-shean stands among the cities recorded in the sad catalogue of Israel’s incomplete obedience, where the people spared what the LORD had bidden them to remove. The most grievous scene in the city’s history came in the day of Saul’s defeat. When the Philistines had slain Saul and his sons in Mount Gilboa, they cut off his head, stripped his armour, and fastened his body and the bodies of his sons to the wall of Beth-shan, and put his armour in the house of their idols. Then the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead, remembering Saul’s kindness to them, arose and went all night and took the bodies from the wall of Beth-shan, and burned them, and buried their bones, and fasted seven days. In Solomon’s reign Beth-shean fell under one of the king’s appointed officers for provision. The city thus joins two solemn themes: the cost of failing to obey God fully in driving out evil, and the dishonor that fell upon a king who departed from the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Canaanite city at the east of the valley of Jezreel where the Philistines fastened Saul’s body to the wall, and which Manasseh could not at first drive out.

expand to see more

BETH-SHEAN, also Beth-shan, a city at the east end of the valley of Jezreel near the Jordan.

Within the allotment of Manasseh, who could not at first drive out its Canaanites (Jos 17:11).

Listed among the cities Manasseh failed to expel (Jdg 1:27).

Where the Philistines fastened Saul’s body to the wall (1Sa 31:10).

The men of Jabesh-gilead took down the bodies and buried them (1Sa 31:12).

Key Scripture

Jos 17:11 — "And Manasseh had in Issachar and in Asher Beth-shean and her towns, and Ibleam and her towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Endor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Taanach and her towns, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns, even three countries."

Jdg 1:27 — "Neither did Manasseh drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and her towns, nor Taanach and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Ibleam and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns: but the Canaanites would dwell in that land."

1Sa 31:10 — "And they put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth: and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan."

1Sa 31:12 — "All the valiant men arose, and went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and came to Jabesh, and burnt them there."

Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is the cost of incomplete obedience in driving out evil, and the dishonor that follows departure from the LORD.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Beth-shean stands first as a warning against half-hearted obedience. Manasseh could not, or would not, drive out the Canaanites but put them to tribute and let them dwell in the land. Sin tolerated and managed rather than slain becomes a snare; the evil left standing in Beth-shean was a wound to Israel’s faithfulness that the LORD had commanded them to avoid.

The city’s walls bore a second, darker witness. There the body of Saul, the king who turned from the LORD and sought the witch of Endor, was hung in shame by the Philistines. Yet even there mercy appeared: the men of Jabesh-gilead honored their fallen king with a costly kindness. Beth-shean thus joins the wages of disobedience with a gleam of covenant loyalty, and bids the believer obey fully and remember the faithful even in their dishonor.

Hebrew Roots

The name means “house of quiet” or “house of rest,” a peaceful title strangely contrasted with the city’s violent place in Saul’s downfall.

expand to see more

Beth-shean — from Hebrew beth she’an, “house of quiet” or “house of rest.”

The element beth means “house,” common in place-names (Beth-el, Beth-lehem).

The latter element is linked to a root for ease, quiet, or security.

Appears in the shortened form Beth-shan in the books of Samuel (1Sa 31:10).

The peaceful name stands in grim irony beside the wall where Saul was hung.

Usage

"Manasseh could not drive out the Canaanites of Beth-shean, but put them to tribute."

"The Philistines fastened the body of Saul to the wall of Beth-shan."

"The valiant men of Jabesh went all night to take the bodies from Beth-shan."
